mcqs: Lyman series (to n = 1) is ultraviolet; Paschen and Brackett (to n = 3, 4) are infrared.
The Balmer series (to n = 2) lies in the visible region.
The longest wavelength of a series comes from the smallest energy jump.
For Balmer (ending at n = 2) that is the transition from n = 3: λ = 656.2 nm (H-α).
Energy needed to remove the electron from n = 2 is 3.4 eV.
From level n the possible transitions to all lower levels number n(n − 1)/2.
X-ray production: kinetic energy of electrons → photon energy.
The photoelectric effect is the reverse: photon energy → kinetic energy of an electron.
Ordinary excited states last about 10⁻⁸ s, but a metastable state lasts much longer, about 10⁻³ s.
This long lifetime makes population inversion possible.
The He-Ne laser emits at 632.8 nm, which is red light.
The He-Ne laser tube is filled with about 85% helium and 15% neon (at low pressure).
Photon energy = difference between the levels.
L-series X-rays are emitted when electrons fall into the L shell (n = 2).
L_α is from n = 3 and L_β from n = 4: n = 4 → n = 2.
Pumping supplies energy to raise atoms to higher (metastable) levels.
Its purpose is to achieve population inversion — more atoms in the upper level than in the lower level.
In Bohr's model mvr = nh/2π and r ∝ n², so v ∝ 1/n.
shortQuestions: A hydrogen sample contains an enormous number of atoms. Different atoms are excited to different energy levels.

Each electron can return to lower levels by many different possible jumps (e.g. 3→2, 3→1, 4→2…). Each kind of jump emits a photon of a particular energy, giving one line. So the spectrum has many lines even though each atom has one electron.

In a solid the atoms are packed closely and interact strongly, so their energy levels broaden into continuous bands; electrons can make transitions of any energy and all wavelengths are emitted — a continuous spectrum (thermal radiation).
In a hot, low-density gas the atoms are far apart and isolated; each has sharp, discrete energy levels, so only definite wavelengths are emitted — a line spectrum.

(a) A photon of less than 13.6 eV is absorbed only if its energy exactly equals the difference between the ground state and an excited state (10.2 eV, 12.09 eV, 12.75 eV, …). Otherwise it is not absorbed.
(b) Yes. Any photon with energy greater than 13.6 eV can be absorbed: it ionises the atom and the extra energy appears as kinetic energy of the freed electron.
E_n = −13.6/n² eV: as n increases the levels get closer together, crowding towards the ionisation limit (E = 0).
So the energy differences, and hence the wavelengths, of successive lines in a series differ less and less, and the lines converge towards the series limit.
By classical electromagnetism an orbiting (accelerating) electron should radiate energy continuously, spiral into the nucleus and give a continuous spectrum — atoms would be unstable.

Bohr postulated that only orbits with angular momentum mvr = nh/2π are allowed, in which the electron does not radiate. This quantisation gives stable orbits with definite energies, explaining the stability of atoms and the line spectrum.
Light comes from transitions of the outer (valence) electrons, involving energy differences of a few eV.
X-rays come from transitions of inner-shell electrons in heavy atoms (after an inner electron is knocked out), involving energies of thousands of eV.
So X-ray photons have much higher energy and shorter wavelength; they are penetrating and ionising, unlike visible light.
(a) Bremsstrahlung (continuous) X-rays: the shortest wavelength λ_min = hc/(eV) decreases, so the continuous spectrum extends to shorter wavelengths (and becomes more intense).

(b) Characteristic X-rays: their wavelengths do not change, because they depend only on the energy levels of the target element; only their intensity increases (and new lines may appear once V exceeds the needed excitation energy).
Diffraction is noticeable only when the wavelength is comparable to the spacing of the 'grating'.

The spacing between atoms in a crystal is about 0.1 nm, comparable to X-ray wavelengths, so crystals diffract X-rays. UV wavelengths (≈ 10–400 nm) are far too long, so no useful diffraction pattern is formed.
longQuestions: When hydrogen gas is excited in a discharge tube, it emits a line spectrum: definite wavelengths arranged in series.
All lines fit the formula 1/λ = R_H(1/p² − 1/n²), with R_H = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ (Rydberg constant), p = 1, 2, 3… and n = p + 1, p + 2, …
Lyman series (p = 1): ultraviolet. Balmer series (p = 2): visible (H-α 656 nm, H-β 486 nm, H-γ 434 nm, H-δ 410 nm). Paschen (p = 3), Brackett (p = 4) and Pfund (p = 5): infrared.
In each series the lines get closer together towards the series limit (n → ∞).
Bohr's theory explains this: each line is a photon emitted when the electron jumps from level n to level p, hf = E_n − E_p.

Bohr's postulates: (1) The electron revolves in certain circular orbits without radiating energy (stationary states). (2) In these orbits the angular momentum is quantised: mvr = nh/2π. (3) Radiation is emitted or absorbed only when the electron jumps between orbits: hf = E_n − E_p.
(a) Radius: the electrostatic force provides the centripetal force: ke²/r² = mv²/r. With v = nh/(2πmr): r_n = n²h²/(4π²mke²) = n² × 0.053 nm.
(b) Energy: K.E. = ½mv² = ke²/(2r), P.E. = −ke²/r, so total E = −ke²/(2r).
Substituting r_n: E_n = −2π²mk²e⁴/(n²h²) = −13.6/n² eV.
The negative energy means the electron is bound; E₁ = −13.6 eV is the ground state.
Ground state: the lowest energy state of an atom (n = 1 for hydrogen, E₁ = −13.6 eV), in which it is most stable.
Excited state: any higher energy state (n = 2, 3, …) reached when the atom absorbs energy; the atom stays there only about 10⁻⁸ s before returning.
Excitation energy: the energy needed to raise an electron from the ground state to an excited state, e.g. 10.2 eV for n = 1 → 2 in hydrogen (the corresponding voltage is the excitation potential).
Ionisation energy: the minimum energy needed to remove the electron completely from the ground state to infinity (E = 0); 13.6 eV for hydrogen (ionisation potential 13.6 V).
X-rays are electromagnetic waves of very short wavelength (about 0.01–10 nm), discovered by Roentgen.

Production: in an X-ray (Coolidge) tube, electrons from a heated filament are accelerated by a high p.d. (tens of kV) and strike a heavy-metal target (tungsten); about 1% of their energy becomes X-rays, the rest heat.

Continuous X-rays (bremsstrahlung): produced when electrons are decelerated by the nuclei of the target; all wavelengths down to λ_min = hc/(eV) occur; λ_min depends on the tube voltage, not the target.

Characteristic X-rays: an incoming electron knocks out an inner-shell (K or L) electron; an outer electron falls into the vacancy, emitting a photon of definite energy (K_α, K_β, L_α…). These sharp lines are characteristic of the target element and do not depend on the voltage.
LASER: Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation — an intense, monochromatic, coherent and highly directional beam.
Principle: stimulated emission. An incoming photon of energy hf = E₂ − E₁ causes an excited atom to emit an identical photon (same frequency, phase and direction), so light is amplified.

Requirements: population inversion (more atoms in the upper level than the lower), produced by pumping into a metastable state (lifetime ≈ 10⁻³ s), and an optical resonator (two parallel mirrors, one partly silvered) to reflect photons back and forth.

He-Ne laser operation: an electric discharge excites He atoms to a metastable level; collisions transfer the energy to Ne atoms, giving population inversion in Ne. Stimulated transitions in Ne emit 632.8 nm red light, which builds up between the mirrors and emerges through the partly silvered mirror.
Uses: surgery, eye operations, CD/DVD players, fibre-optic communication, holography, cutting and welding.
